utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, Counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Ms. Tecla Henry-Benjamin, Daryl Mundis, and the case manager, Mr. Andres Vatter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Appearances for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of General Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, counsel; Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel; and Muriel Cauvin, case manager.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic and Nermin Mulalic, legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber would like to welcome everybody present in the courtroom, the Prosecution, the Defence counsel, the accused, and everybody else. You have all noticed that we have had a delay due to a technical glitch which did not allow us to begin at 9.00. As the President of this Chamber who has the responsibility to secure the smooth proceedings, I would like to ask the registrar to make sure that half an hour before the beginning of the session that a technician comes and checks every detail in the courtroom to make sure that everything works. Can you imagine a situation in which we had the press, the general public, and everybody waiting for the session to begin at 9.00 and then there is a delay? That's why I would kindly ask you to make sure that a technician is present in due time to check that everything works in the courtroom at least half an hour before the session. We would like to avoid such accidents in the future. The Chamber would like to render a decision regarding a document which was tendered into evidence. This was the "Instructions to the Muslim Fighter." As you know, we have given it a number for identification. It was P11 ID. This document was presented to the witness and the witness did not recognise the whole document. He only recognised page 25. The Chamber has deliberated and decided that an exhibit number will be given to the front page and the pages 24 and 25 of this document. The remainder of this document still needs to be identified. This is the decision that we are rendering on this document which was given a number for identification, P11 ID. So we would like to have an exhibit number for the flyleaf and pages 24 and 25 of this document. Today we have a witness who has been envisaged, but before that, Mr. Registrar, can you please confirm that this document has an exhibit number and that it will be admitted into evidence under number P11.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the pages you mentioned get the exhibit number P11.1 and P11.1/E for the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. We still have to be provided with these pages by the Prosecution, because for the time being they haven't been officially provided to the Chamber. Can you please provide these pages to the registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, we will provide the pages during the course of today's proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Madam Usher, can you please bring the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. I would like to check whether you can hear the interpretation of my words into English. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have been called as a Prosecution witness. You're going to take the solemn declaration in order to testify, but before that, could you please give us your name, the date of birth, the place of birth, and your nationality.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Major Angus Hay, born 19/3/1967, born Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, and I'm a Brit Scot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Currently a ground liaison officer with the Royal Air Force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where are you stationed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Royal Air Force Lossiemouth in the north of Scotland.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your rank, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Major.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1993, 11 years ago, you were in Bosnia and Herzegovina. In what position did you serve and what was your rank there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was a captain attached to the Prince of Wales' Own BritBat 2, where I was a military liaison officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you already testified either before an international tribunal or before a national court about the events which took place during the year 1993, or is this your first testimony before a court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have been here before, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please tell us whether you have testified once, two times. How many times have you testified and in which case, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have only been in the court once, and that was against Mr. Kordic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Were you a Prosecution witness or a Defence witness when you testified?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A Prosecution witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could you please read the text of the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Major, you may be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for the delay, which was due to a technical glitch in the courtroom. You have been called to testify. First you're going to be asked questions by the Prosecution, and after that the Defence is going to lead their cross-examination. They're also going to ask you questions, and their time will be limited to 50 per cent of the time given to the Prosecution. After the second stage, once the Defence has finished their questioning, the Prosecution may wish to re-examine you. The three Judges seated before you, if they think it may be necessary to put questions to you in order to clarify matters or to fill in gaps in your answers, may also put questions to you. Generally speaking, the Judges prefer to wait until the Prosecution and the Defence have finished with their examination and cross-examination. When the Judges put questions to you, they will give the floor to the Defence and to the Prosecution to ask questions that might arise from the Judges' questions. Try to answer as concisely and as precisely as possible to the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. questions put to you. As you know, we are in the so-called oral procedure and your testimony is the most important thing. I would also like to remind you of two or three other points which do not necessarily apply to you. First of all, you have taken an oath to tell the truth, which means that you have taken an oath not to give a false testimony, which is punishable under the law. And the second point I would like to raise is that a witness may sometimes decide not to answer a question put to him because such an answer might incriminate the witness. In such a case, the Chamber may compel the witness to answer; however, when doing that, the Chamber will guarantee such a witness a sort of immunity. This is in a nutshell how your testimony will develop. Without wasting any more time, since we have already wasted 45 minutes due to the technical problem, I am giving the floor to the Prosecution, and I believe it is going to be Mrs. Benjamin who's going to lead the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Good morning, Major Hay. You would have indicated previously to the Trial Chamber your rank and -- your present rank and your rank while you were in Bosnia. Could you briefly state for the Chamber your military qualifications and experience, if any, please.

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: Could you elaborate on that again, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Where did you receive your training in your career?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: I joined the army in 1983 as a boy soldier with the British Army. I was commissioned in 1988, spending a year at the Royal Military Academy Sandhurst, after which I joined the Gordon Highlanders which is an infantry battalion, and I've been in the army now for 21 years.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Prior to your deployment to Bosnia, did you receive any training in preparation for the said deployment?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We did a number of weeks or a couple of months build-up training prior to deployment. That was both in -- basically in Germany, culminating in an exercise and training finalisation based in Sennelager.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could you please state for the Trial Chamber, Major, your duration of the tour of your duty, when it commenced and when it ended.

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: I can't exactly remember. It was around about end of May, beginning of -- end of April, beginning of May 1993. And I finished my tour of duty October/November. I can't remember precisely. It was approximately seven months.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. And kindly state for us your area of responsibility whilst in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: When we first arrived, the liaison officer that I took over from had a real estate spanning from Busovaca, Vitez, Zenica, Novi Travnik, Travnik, Turbe. But after two and a half, three weeks in theatre, we realised -- I realised that it was unworkable and consequently my area of responsibility was reduced down to the area of Turbe, Travnik, and Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. As a BritBat liaison officer, could you briefly state for us what was the role or the purpose of BritBat in Bosnia at the time.

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: The purpose of BritBat was to assist with the distribution of humanitarian aid, working for the United Nations. My responsibility within that was as a military liaison officer to establish working relationships with all the local belligerent commanders and prominent people from all ethnic backgrounds, to establish a working relationship in order to assist with the United Nations furthered missions of humanitarian aid, distribution, monitoring prisoners of war, trying to sort of resolve issues, trying to sort of stop fighting, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: In the process of carrying out your responsibilities, would you have had to participate in meetings of any kind?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: Yes. That was part and parcel of the job, either attending meetings or setting up the said meetings.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: As a result of these meetings, did you have cause to come in contact with the commanders or the senior officers of the units in your AOR at the time?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: Yes. As I've already said, that part of my job was to establish links with all the local commanders as much as I -- as many as I could get access to and prominent people for the said purpose of establishing meetings and just building a working relationship with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Now, could you tell us some of the commanders that you may have met with while on the tour of your duty.

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: I can safely say that I came into contact with most of the sort of prominent individuals from the sort of Lasva Valley, centred around Vitez, up to Zenica, Travnik, Novi Travnik. Basically all the local commanders from all the -- from both the HVO and the BiH side.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Major Hay, could you state for the Trial Chamber the units that were present in your AOR at that time.

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: I cannot remember all of the units and I can't -- my mind is a bit murky on -- as far as the specific HVO units go, because really after the sort of first two and a half, three weeks the majority of my sort of real estate encompassed the ABiH centred around Travnik, of which there came under command 3 Corps; there was, I think, 17 Krajina Brigade, 7th Muslim Brigade. And I can't remember the other ones, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Apart from the three that you have mentioned, were there any other units present in your AOR that you may -- that may have come under the ABiH, as far as you're aware?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: There was -- sorry, could you elaborate on that?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Well, you told us that you saw the 3rd Corps, the 17th, and the 7th. Did you see any other soldiers in the AOR at that time?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: As I said, yes, but I can't remember specific designations what units they belonged to, specific badges or anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. In the conduct of your meetings, did you at any time have any dealings with Mr. Enver Hadzihasanovic?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: I met Mr. Hadzihasanovic a couple of times during my sort of first month in Central Bosnia, specifically when I was taking over from the LO with the Cheshires, because his real estate encompassed Zenica. And then really when my area of responsibility was reduced, I really didn't have many meetings with him after that. I may have met him at a couple of meetings, but I really didn't have anything -- any direct sort of contact with him.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could you therefore, then, assist the Trial Chamber from a professional point of view and from a military standpoint your opinion of the individual Enver Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: My opinion of Mr. Hadzihasanovic was he was the commander of 3 Corps. That is what we were led to believe, and consequently that's what I was led to believe. He commanded 3 Corps from Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And would you have cause to meet Mr. Alagic?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: In the course of your meetings?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Alagic was my daily contact basically, really. I had a lot of dealings with Mr. Alagic.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could you, then, Major, give us again your professional assessment and personal assessment with respect to Mr. Alagic.

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: Mr. Alagic was, I believe, a former JNA army officer. He was a larger-than-life character, but he was very shrewd.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: One of your -- okay, during your tenure, one of your duties - I presume, and correct me if I'm wrong - one of your duties was to receive complaints and to relay such complaints with the respective commanders that you met. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: In doing so, what would be the response of, for example, Mr. Alagic, to these complaints?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: Just to clarify, these allegations, rumours, whatever, ranged from atrocities to mutilations, to somebody was fighting on some front, did we know this, did we know that, et cetera. Anyway, Mr. Alagic's Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. response depended on the situation and would change on a daily basis, obviously depending on the overall situation as he perceived it. He could be helpful. He could be uncooperative. He could deny it. It just depended on the situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: But would you say at all times your responsibility was to bring it to his attention as to what complaints you'd received and would you say that you always did this and he was always put on notice with respect to all the complaints you may have received? Would you say so?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: I think my colleague is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honours. Good day, Mr. President. Mr. President, the last three questions are leading questions. They're trying to obtain a specific answer from the witness. The last three questions -- although I'm ready to allow my colleagues certain room for manoeuvre, these last three questions are leading and the witness should really be allowed to answer of his own accord without being led. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What could the Prosecution say? When we have a look at the way the question was phrased in the transcript, it's true that the witness doesn't have much room for manoeuvre when answering the question put to him. We could obtain the same results by asking the question -- by asking the witness shorter questions. And since the witness saw one of the two accused and the person called Alagic who is now deceased, you could ask him whether he was able to provide you with certain information with regard to certain matters. Ms. Benjamin, given what Mr. Bourgon has said, could you rephrase the question without leading the witness. I know that everyone wants to save time, and going to the substance could make this possible, but nevertheless there are certain rules that have to be respected. These rules may be restrictive, but we have to establish a balance between the need to save time and the need to respect rules which might be restrictive. So Ms. Benjamin, please rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. But the witness, having already established the foundation that he was in company with the commander during the meetings, I thought it could just follow on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Major Hay, in the course of your meetings, could you tell the Trial Chamber where the meetings were held?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: The locations of the meetings changed according to what was happening around the ground. We tried to -- I remember attending meetings in, as we called it, the JNA barracks, Alagic's headquarters in Travnik. We attended meetings in one of the hotels in Travnik where the ECMM based themselves for a while. And we also convened some of the meetings when the atmosphere and the environment became a little bit more hostile. We chaired a couple of meetings at the school where we were based.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And specifically with respect to Mr. Alagic's headquarters, did you have cause to visit any other place whilst there?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: Sorry, within his headquarters?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: Yes. We -- myself and my brother, we visited, or we were taken down to visit a detention centre underneath his headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And could you kindly tell the Trial Chamber your observations on this visit, please.

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: It was a cellar. There were detainees in it. I can't remember exactly how many, who they were, but there was nothing that drew mine or my brother's attention out of the ordinary. They were reasonably -- in reasonable condition, et cetera. There was lighting, and if I remember rightly, there was some medical facilities down there. But there was nothing horrific or draconian, if I remember rightly.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Did you see detainees in the centre?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: Yes. Or alleged detainees.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. And would you be able to assist us with the ethnic background of these detainees?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: I cannot remember. I can't even remember if Alagic told us who they were. I'm sure he did. But I could only assume that they would have been HVO, apart from one chap up top, who was a detainee who was one of his own military commanders.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: In the summer of 1993, how would you describe the atmosphere in your AOR at that time?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: Tense.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could you elaborate for us, please.

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: This is from my own perspective. We arrived, the POW took over from the Cheshires a few weeks after the bomb went off in the centre of Vitez and also subsequently the -- what happened at Ahmici. And really, just maybe not necessarily as direct result of that but a cascading effect following on from that, the relationship between Croats and Muslims just deteriorated, and deteriorated the longer we were based in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Major Hay, did there come a time when you began to see the emergence of other units in your AOR? Did there come a time?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: To that, I presume you are or you will be referring to what we, BritBat, basically the foreign element, the foreign mercenaries, Mujahedin, as the Croats referred to them. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could you please state for the Trial Chamber what, if anything, that you learnt of this group of people. What did you learn about them?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: They were definitely foreign mercenaries. I personally saw a number of them, deceased individuals of North African and Middle Eastern persuasion. They were, we believe, a sort of spearhead -- or used as the initiators of any sort of ABiH sort of offensive. That's what the purpose of their being there was, we believed. And for some reason - I can't remember why - we associated them with 7 Muslim Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: During your tour of duty, could you briefly summarise your observations with respect to the two armies and their relationships; that being the ABiH and the HVO.

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: Compared to each other or ...?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Yes. What did you observe about the relations and what transpired between the two?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: The BiH -- I'm sorry, I'm not entirely sure what you're after here.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Did both parties -- did both armies have a good relationship between them?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: Not particularly as time went on.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And as time went on, what did you observe?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: Well, the hostilities increased and frequency of sort of fighting increased.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: What about the complaints that would relayed to you? Did they increase?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: I think they probably did, given the frequency of events increasing, the number of events, you know. As a result, allegations, fact or false, you know, were rife.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And as a result of these increased reports, alleged incidents, what was your role? What role did you play respect to quelling same or sorting same out? What role did you play?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: Going back to the beginning of the questioning, one of my roles -- one of the key roles was relaying these concerns to the local commanders, putting the facts as they were presented to us or the allegations as they were presented to us factually or fictionally, putting them to the local commanders, seeing what the response was, asking what they were going to do about it. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And so I'll go back to the original question, if I'm allowed to go. What was the response of the local commanders to your reports? And maybe you could tell us which commanders and the response.

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: I go back to my earlier answer too, insofar as -- and it wasn't just General Alagic. It was Sablic Jeliko [phoen], the ABiH commander from Novi Travnik; there was Salko Beba, there was the HVO commanders in Travnik. I can't remember their names now. The response differed on a daily basis. They wanted to use us to their advantage, if possible. Sometimes that wasn't possible. They didn't believe us sometimes. Some of the rumours and allegations were just beyond fantasy. Some of them, you know, applied a bit of common sense to it. There was a basis to it. And their response differed on a daily basis. Sometimes they could be cooperative, they wanted us to pursue issues; other times they would just deny things happened if the allegations were against them, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Major, how, then, would you describe your tour of duty if you had to sum it up in one word? How would you describe it?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: Frustrating.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Frustrating meaning that you did not achieve your ends or your goals?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: I think we achieved a lot. But what one must appreciate was there was a war going on in Central Bosnia there and, you know, the situation isn't made easier by that. Our duty.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Frustrating because you didn't get the action that you thought may have occurred? Why frustrating? That's the point I want to get. Why do you describe it as frustrating?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: You leave the base with a mission in mind and -- or something to do, and you may achieve it or you may not. And a whole host of other things would come onto the horizon that you'd have to deal with on a daily basis. It was shuttle diplomacy and you just reacted to situations as they arose, of which there were many every day.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours. This concludes the examination-in-chief. Thank you, Major.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Ms. Benjamin. It took you about 30 minutes to conduct your examination-in-chief. Mr. Bourgon, I can see you with your lectern. So you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] Good morning, Mr. Hay. We have had the pleasure of meeting yesterday, and I'd like to take this opportunity for thank you for taking the time to meet with us yesterday. Let me begin by introducing myself for the benefit of the transcript as well as my two colleagues. I am accompanied this morning by Mrs. Edina Residovic as well as Mrs. Muriel Cauvin, and together we represent General Hadzihasanovic. I only have a few questions for you this morning, Major, and I think this should not take too long. Let me begin by asking if you can confirm that you gave a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor in April of 1997. Do you recall giving a statement?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: I've given about two or three statements or two statements, I think. The first one, the time frame sounds about right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I go straight into some of the specifics that you've raised today. You mentioned that you had daily dealings with a gentleman called Alagic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You mentioned the time when you went to see Mr. Alagic at his headquarters, which was located in the JNA barracks.

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you also referred to a fact that you visited some kind of a detention facility which was below his headquarters; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, just for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, in response to a question by my colleague you mentioned that you were accompanied by your brother at the time. Can you confirm that your brother, Colin Hay, was occupying at the time similar functions as yours as a United Kingdom liaison officer in the same area as you were?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And this is the reason why both yourself and your brother visited Mr. Alagic.

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can you confirm, Major, that on that occasion your visit to Mr. Alagic had not been announced before?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: Yes. I think I can confirm that. We never really announced our visits. We just sort of dropped in when we were doing our sort of rounds. We never really sort of set a time or anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And on that specific day, Major, the fact that you visited the detention facility was done at your own request and initiative.

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: I can't remember who initiated it, but -- I can't confirm that. I can't remember who initiated the visit, i.e., to the detention centre, I can't remember -- Alagic sort of said, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Major, do you recall that you were asked similar questions when you testified in the Kordic case before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: Again, I can't remember specifics. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But you do recall testifying.

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I would just like to read you your answer, and then you can tell me whether the answer you provided then fits with what you still believe today.

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, the question that was put to you at that time --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm referring to the transcript of the testimony of Major Hay in the Blaskic case. It's on page 10, 296 -- I apologise, the Kordic case, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] The question that was put to you again, Major, was: "In the course of 1993, you had occasion to visit General Alagic in Travnik and his headquarters." And your answer was yes. And then the further question was: "You noticed in the basement of these headquarters the presence of HVO prisoners. Could you describe -- tell us what conditions they appeared to be in." And your answer was, "Yes, they were in a reasonable settle given the fact that they were prisoners of war, but they were being looked after and they did not -- there was nothing untowards that I recall." Would that be a fair statement of what you would believe today?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: Yes. But as time goes on, my mind gets murkier of events, so that is a timely reminder.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The next question which was put to you was: "Had you announced your visit to General Alagic beforehand?" And your answer to this question was: "No, he was unaware that I would be arriving and he took he me down at my request and showed me around and during then was when I was introduced to the prisoners of war." Would that be --

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: That sounds about right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, this morning you mentioned in response to a question by my colleague that you saw in this facility some medical facilities.

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: Yes, I mentioned it. I can't remember exactly -- something rings a bell that there was a medical facility or there was -- there was some medical equipment down there, if I remember rightly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you also mentioned that you saw the detainees and that you assume they were HVO. Now, other than the fact that they were well treated, as you said, you don't know whether they were HVO and they could have been detainees from the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: They could have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you also mentioned in response to a question by my colleague that "There was one of his own commanders who was there at the time." Are you referring to the commander -- or who are you referring to when you say "there was one of his own commanders there"?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: It was a chap by the name of Mr. Berberovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And do you know why he was there?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: I remember the -- being told by Alagic that there had been some fratricide basically, a blue-on-blue. He had killed some of his own people, a mistake with an artillery piece or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Moving on, Major Hay. You mentioned that the atmosphere in 1993 was tense. And you answered then that you had some information about the presence of foreign mercenaries.

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, on this issue of foreign mercenaries, would I be right in saying that what you believed at the time is that you did not know -- and I read here from your statement -- you did not know who formally controlled the Mujahedin and who coordinated their activities? Would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: That is right. I can't remember why, but within BritBat, it was the intelligence officer, whatever, but somehow we associated them with 7 Muslim Brigade. But actual coordination, control, ownership of them was never really tied down.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you yourself, other than knowing -- you did not know where these people came from and when they came into Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: No, not exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you did not know exactly where they were located in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: We saw small pockets of them, and in particular -- I can't remember the name of the building, but as you come into Travnik on the right-hand side from Vitez, as you just come into Travnik, there was a building that -- again, for some reason, I can't remember -- we associated with these foreign elements, and also up in the high country sort of between Travnik and Zenica, the back road to Travnik and Zenica, Guca Gora area, out in the sort of outcountry there, there was a -- small pockets of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, Major, I'd like to refer you again to your testimony in the Kordic case, when a question was put to you concerning units or parts of units operating individually. And the question which was put to you was: "Did you obtain clear information of which commander, regardless of whether he was from the HVO or from the BH army, was responsible for which particular area?" And your response to this question - and I quote from line 24 of the transcript - your response was: "Furthermore, regarding your question, there was a lot of provincial, local individuals who may have been doing things on their own without the consent, knowledge, or whatever of the hierarchy on both sides." Would that be a fair statement of your experience --

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: Yes, it would.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: With respect to Mr. Alagic, you mentioned in response to a question that his reaction on a daily basis would depend on the pace of the operational scenario, would it?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: Yes, it depended on the situation on the ground. It depended on what was happening, what had happened to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, yesterday when we met and we discussed this question, you made reference to the fact that Commander Alagic was making and doing the best he could in a most difficult and demanding times. Would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: Looking at it from his perspective, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Let me move on to a quick question concerning something that you referred to in your testimony in the Kordic case, and that was the Convoy of Joy. Do you remember this convoy?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I would like to quote you in terms of what you mentioned in the Kordic transcript concerning the Convoy of Joy, to see whether you can recall your testimony. The question that was put to you then - and I quote from page 10289 - was as follows: "What did you establish about the circumstances on which the convoy was diverted?" And your answer was: "It was no secret that there was a convoy coming up, as we called it then, at Route Diamond, and it was apprehended, stopped at the Novi Travnik -- Novi Travnik sort of junction, into Novi Travnik by a woman with sort of sticks and goodness knows what. They stopped the whole convoy. We were aware of it, but our mandate prevented us from doing anything at that time. And unfortunately we were sort of caught between a brick and a hard place -- or a rock and a hard place, and as soon as it stopped, a number of drivers were dragged -- taken out of their cabs, and allegedly shot straightaway." Do you recall that this is something that had happened and that people responsible for this event were members of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And going on in this testimony, you referred to the fact that the convoy was then looted and that some vehicles were taken away from this convoy.

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you recall this event? I'd like you to -- yesterday I, having a discussion with you, because you were in Travnik -- Sorry, Major, your last response to my question concerning the fact whether you recalled this event is not -- was not recorded in the transcript. So I'll simply put my question again to you, in the sense of were you aware of the fact that the convoy was looted and that some vehicles were actually stolen and taken away from the convoy and all this was committed by members of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yesterday, Major, we discussed because of your presence in Travnik whether you were aware of any kidnappings taking place in Travnik around September/October, and you mentioned to me that you had no recollection of any such events.

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: I can't remember, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I just have maybe one last question for you, and that was with respect to those Mujahedin that we were referring to. You never spoke to any Mujahedin, did you?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Major. That concludes my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have now concluded my cross-examination on behalf of General Hadzihasanovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. The other Defence team, do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We do not have any questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Prosecution, any re-examination for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think I just have one question.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Major Hay, you said that there came a time when you associated the so-called foreigners, Mujahedins, with the 7th Muslim Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This question has already been asked during the examination-in-chief, and I don't see any use for putting this question again to the same witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Benjamin, any re-examination should arise from the cross-examination. I suppose that the other Defence team would like to say something about the same issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we would also like to say that the witness has already replied two or three times during the examination-in-chief and during the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: That's just the point, Mr. President. It was raised again in cross-examination and I wanted to clear it up again in re-examination. But if my friends have a problem, then the Prosecution rests. We have no re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. The first stage is over and the Judges have some questions for you, sir. The Judge who's sitting to my left is going to start.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Let me just say a few follow-up questions, Witness, on your visit to the detention centre in the JNA barracks. It seems that you have testified before on the issue in the Kordic case, and that was some years ago, I suppose. I just wonder, what made you go to the Travnik barracks in order to visit the detention centre? Had you any reason for doing so, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I can't remember specifically. But I would visit the -- Alagic on a daily basis, really. I can't remember whether we were given any specific information or intelligence that -- to have a look there. I can't recall now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So you have hardly any remembrance of the event at all, is my understanding.

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: My memory of the events is fading, Your Honour. That was a reminder from the last time I was here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Well, apparently in the -- during your testimony in the Kordic case you have said that you saw HVO soldiers, and today you said "I cannot remember what kind of prisoners they were." I suppose you don't remember why you said that they were HVO soldiers when you testified in the Kordic case?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, I'm sorry, I can't sort of elaborate. I can't remember. I really can't remember now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Well, if you can't remember, you can't remember. I won't blame you for that. The second point that was raised was your meetings with commanders from both sides in which you raised allegations, rumours, that kind of things and submitted them to these commanders, either HVO or ABiH, and you mentioned also the responses you got. Sometimes they were inclined to listen to you; sometimes they were inclined to deny rumours or allegations, or -- you gave a sort of picture of that. My question is: Do you remember specific instances in which you reported rumours or allegations to, for example, Alagic?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- again, now I can't remember specifics, other than a general overview of what may have been happening on a monthly basis regarding rumours of mutilations, body exchanges, prisoner of war conditions. But I can't remember any specifics, Your Honour. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Major, in reply to a question put to you a little while ago concerning Mujahedins spoke about having seen fighters who had been killed. Can you confirm that that was indeed the essence of your reply? Were you present? Were you there? Did you see the Mujahedin who were killed during a battle?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: Yes, I did, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what were the circumstances that brought you to see those bodies? What were the circumstances of that event? What was the occasion? How did you come to see the dead people?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: There were two separate occasions; one where I physically saw the bodies, another one I was given a tape recording by the HVO of an ambush that had just taken place before. The incident where I specifically saw the bodies was at Rastovici, just to the south of Novi Travnik on Route Diamond, as we called the route. There had been an offensive -- the day before, the evening before. I cannot remember exactly now -- where the HVO had repelled an offensive by the ABiH. I can't remember what the objective of the attack was or whatever. But consequently they killed a number of the ABiH or the mercenaries, the foreign Mujahedin. And there was a number of them lying on the ground. There was four or five laid out in one area, and there was about another three, as I say, I think it was a total of eight, on the back of a tractor. And I physically saw the bodies there, and they were definitely of North African, Middle Eastern persuasion. They were not indigenous to Central Bosnia. And if I remember rightly -- I can't remember now the specifics, but they did have sort of paperwork on them. Whether it was identification or not, I cannot remember now, that corroborated this. And for some reason I recall a Ugandan, somebody from Sudan, a Saudi Arabian, if I remember rightly, and there was a whole host of others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you be more precise about the date when this happened, the day, the month? When was it? What month was it, at least?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, I can't recall now. It was towards the end of my tour though, and I left sort of end of October/November. It may have been sort of a bracket date, sort of mid-September onwards. I cannot remember specifically, Your Honour. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And on that day, you just happened to be there? What was the motive of your presence on that spot, on the spot of the battle that had taken place either a few days or a few hours before you arrived there? Why did you go there in the first place? What was the reason?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: I was taken there by the local HVO commanders. I remember Sablic Jeliko telling me that this had happened and they were obviously sort of a couple who were quite proud of what had happened. And, of course, the other side of the corps and everybody there, both sides, were paranoid about allegations of atrocities and things. And I, if I remember rightly, he wanted to sort of show me and prove, you know, that no atrocity had been done to these bodies, no mutilations or anything, so he wanted to show me them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand you well, you were in the area of responsibility of the HVO. So this area us under the control of the HVO. Am I right in thinking that?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: Yes. And I had obviously visited the local HVO commander in Novi Travnik and he'd told me that this had happened, and it was a conflict line just bordering sort of ABiH and HVO territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're a professional soldier and you had a technical eye, so to speak. And when you saw four or five bodies lying there, what was the uniform that they had on? Were they civilians? Were they soldiers? Could you describe the appearance of those bodies? As far as you can remember. What about their clothes?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: They were in uniform. They were different from the normal ABiH soldiers that I'd been working with over a period of months in Central Bosnia. They were different. They stood out. They were just more professional and narrowed a small specific incident or item -- the rations that they had, I remember now. They were all equipped the same. There was no real difference between them. They had their sort of rations on them and the same armaments, same uniform, et cetera. They were -- there was something about them. They stood out. They were different. Just more professional.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you see any insignia on their uniforms, any patches? Was there anything specific, in terms of insignia on their uniforms?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I cannot remember. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as their weapons are concerned, did you notice any weapons? Were there any weapons lying around them? Or maybe there was a person who was there with you on behalf of the HVO told you that there had been weapons recovered from those bodies. Can you remember?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: If -- I can't remember specifics, but I believe there were weapons. I think it was AK-47s. I can't remember if each one had one or what, but -- there were weapons there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems that you have already told us that they had some IDs on them. Did you see those IDs? I believe that the HVO soldiers had searched those bodies in order to find some elements of identification. Did you yourself see those documents that had been found on the bodies of those fighters?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: I can't say I didn't. I can't recollect exactly what happened, because incidents -- subsequent incidents took over my presence there and we had to get out of there very quickly because we started coming under fire. But I believe that I was shown some documentation. I can't remember exactly what it is or what it was, but it would have been in the milinfosums from the day that we submitted to our higher formation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You also said that on another occasion, on the second occasion, you also saw Mujahedin, and you said that there was a video. Could you tell us something about the second occasion on which you saw the Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: I never actually physically saw them, the bodies. All I saw was the aftermath, a -- basically a local sort of camcorder of the event taken by the local HVO, again in Novi Travnik. I believe the circumstances surrounding it were a small 4 by 4 vehicle with four foreign fighters, Mujahedin, had crossed a conflict line by mistake up Route Diamond and had somehow accidentally gone into Novi Travnik. I don't think they realised the danger they were in, but subsequently the local Croats, HVO or whoever in Novi Travnik sent them on a wild goose chase or deliberately put them down a road where they were ambushed. And three of the four individuals were killed in the car, and I believe one of them was taken prisoner or escaped. I can't remember exactly which now. But again, the HVO, although I didn't physically see it, I had the video footage of it and there was documentation and paperwork on that video footage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And my last question: On a number of occasions you said that they were mercenaries. As you yourself are a professional soldier, what would your definition of a mercenary be? In your opinion, what is a mercenary exactly?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: A mercenary is a -- a soldier who gets paid for -- paid -- sorry. A mercenary is everything that I'm not basically, Your Honour, a soldier of fortune; a soldier who fights for his own ideals or other ideals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And such a mercenary, in your opinion, can such a mercenary be part of a regular army? Is this something that can happen?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: In a nutshell, no. But what was happening in Central Bosnia at the time, you know, one couldn't really apply a lot of, you know, reality and common sense and stuff to what was going on out there a lot of the time. That's all I can say, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And as you also had contact with the HVO, do you know whether the HVO had mercenaries among its troops?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: I have no reason to deny that they didn't. In fact, I believe they may have, yes. But applying the -- sorry, maybe applying the term "mercenary" to what was going on out there, it may be inaccurate, because in my experience it was very difficult to tell, you know, going back to indigenous ethnic groups within Bosnia, it was very difficult to tell the difference between local troops, local militia, and civilians. Everybody carried guns. Everybody had a uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Just a few minutes ago you spoke about video footage of the second incident which the HVO showed you. If I recall this well, you said, "I had it in my possession." Now, there is one the list of exhibits a videotape coming apparently from you. Is this the same videotape or not?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: It will be, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: It's the same videotape.

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: It will be, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: That is called a "Balkan Winter" or something like that. Could you tell me something about that video?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: It's a compilation of a variety of video footage, both taken by the military media ops when I was out there and also coverage from the BBC reporters who were out there at the time, the whole gamut of sort of -- not necessarily BBC, international media as well. It's unique footage, all compiled onto one tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So this is not something you made yourself, I understand well?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: No, it's not. It's a compilation that -- I can't remember who -- exactly who made them, but the footage of the ambush is on there as well, or the -- just the immediate aftermath of the ambush as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the HVO video we talked about was given to you?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: And you yourself made this compilation of ...?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: No. Sablic Jeliko gave it to me somehow. I can't remember how I actually got it onto the tape. I think media ops or the BBC helped out there and put it onto the tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: But you did the compilation yourself or was that someone else from the BritBat?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: No. It was -- it was the milinfocell, the media ops cell part of the BritBat who did one tape, and the BBC did another tape. So I've got two tapes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: And when did you give it to the Prosecution, the tape?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: I haven't given it to this Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: You didn't give it to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: No. It was already -- it was from the Kordic trial. It was already here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Did you personally see or view this videotape? Did you see any of the excerpts?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: Sorry, did I see any of the what?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you see any of the excerpts, extracts from the video? Did you see the video?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I've watched the videos, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you are telling us that it consists of two parts. One was made by the media ops from the army; I assume that that relates to the British Army. And the other part was compiled by the BBC. So there are two parts that this video consists of, the part from the army media ops and the part from the BBC.

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour. There are actually two videos, two separate videos.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are there any further questions from the Defence? If so, we will have a break and we will resume after the break. Very well. It's five to 11.00. We will now adjourn and we will resume at twenty-five past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will now resume, and counsel may take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Major, I just have a few additional questions in response to the questions which were asked by the Trial Chamber, and I'd like to begin with the issue first of the detainees you saw in the Travnik barracks, and I fully understand that of course your memory might be fading after more than ten years. But if I would say to you that in the statement that you provided to the Office of the Prosecutor in 1997 and in 2001 you did not mention whether these people were either members of the HVO or members of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, would that be a true statement?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: Sorry, I can just clarify that I didn't mention --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: That you did not in both statements provided to the Office of the Prosecution, you did not mention whether these detainees were either members of the HVO or members of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly what I stated now. I can't remember at the moment, now, who they were. I cannot remember what I said in my statement. But I think my obvious conclusion at the time was that they would have been HVO, given that they were in an ABiH detention centre. That's the only sort of common-sense application I can put onto it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, what you do know, however, is that there was one detainee whom you do remember, and that was Mr. Berberovic, who was definitely a member of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: Yes. And he was outside -- he was up walking --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you do remember seeing 15 to 20 detainees well treated in an area where there was some type of medical facilities.

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you did not speak to any of those detainees.

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you say that Commander Alagic must have told you who they were but you don't remember.

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: I'm sure he must have, yes. Yes. It would make sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I move to the incidents where you say that you saw some dead bodies. I'd like to -- first to the first incident, the one which is on a video. Can you confirm that you were not present when the events pictured on this video took place?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: Correct. I confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that what you recall from this event is that there were four foreigners in a vehicle who drove by mistake in HVO territory.

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: Yes. That is what we believed happened and also confirmed by the HVO. That's what they told us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that one of those people stopped and asked for information, probably because he did not know where he was, and then they were shot on sight.

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: That is basically the gist of what -- that is what we were told by the HVO happened. They weren't necessarily shot on sight. They were set down a road where there was an ambush set up for them, supposedly. That's what we were told.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, Major, you don't know who these people were, their ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: I never saw them physically, just what was on that video footage.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you don't know what they were doing driving this vehicle.

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you don't know since when they had been in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in fact, you don't know any other details about this incident other than you saw four dead bodies.

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: Other than what I saw on the video footage and what the HVO had told us, which ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I move to the second incident, Major. You spoke about an offensive operation being conducted towards Novi Travnik. That's what we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: That's right. Specifically the village of Rastovici, just at the south of Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned in response to a question from the Presiding Judge that you went to see the local HVO commander and that he took you towards those bodies; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Would you recall, Major, that in fact the fighting had stopped and when you were taken to these bodies it was the next day?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: Yes. The time frame, I can't specifically remember. But also -- I'm sorry to bring this up now, but I do remember at the same time there was one to have UN convoys the same incident -- the same conflict, one of the UNHCR drivers or one of the -- I can't remember specifically what convoy it was. A civilian driver had been killed as well and his vehicle was in -- side of the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you mentioned this in your testimony on the Kordic case where this driver was killed by a stray bullet.

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: He was killed. I don't know -- I can't really accurately say whether it was a stray bullet, deliberately, or what. But he was killed, as I believe -- if I remember rightly, told by certainly the HVO that he had been killed as the ABiH offensive had been launched.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, when you saw those bodies, would it be fair to say that you stayed there a very short time because you immediately came under small-arms fire, which was then followed by mortar fire, and that you were to extract from this area very rapidly?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: It was a very tense and scary moment, in fact, when they started shooting --

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- at the place where you were.

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that there were -- the bodies were wearing some type of uniform but you can't recall, in answer to a question from the Presiding Judge, that they had any unit patches.

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: I can't recall. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you don't know if the place you were taken where you saw the bodies, whether this was in fact the place where the bodies had been killed or whether those bodies had been scattered from other areas.

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: It was my interpretation from what had happened on the ground according to what we were briefed by the HVO where we had seen the build-up of these troops the preceding sort of few days, a week or so, it was in or around that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: That area in general.

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: The area in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But you don't know if it was exactly whether the bodies were to you.

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you mentioned that there were some weapons, but you don't know if there were enough weapons for each body. So you can't recall the specifics about the weapons.

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact detail of the weapons, but there were weapons there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And as far as this fighting which went on in that time frame, you did not know either how many people had been killed and belonging to which army.

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: No. I can't remember getting any detailed information on exactly how many had been killed, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And about the type of wounds that these bodies had, you never had time to look at those wounds, because it was such a short time.

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you don't know, if I suggest to you, that when these people actually died, the time of death. You did not know.

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: I'm an expert on this, but I remember looking at the eyes and they were not dead that long. I'm not talking days here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in fact, even if you look at those bodies today, you cannot remember if they were wearing beards or not.

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: Yes. There was a couple with beards.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Maybe some with, some without?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: Yes. If I remember rightly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you have no idea what happened to these bodies once you extracted from this moment.

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: No, I don't know what happened subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you are aware, Major, that propaganda was used as a very effective weapon by the HVO. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ANGUS HAY
utterances.text: It was used as a very effective weapon by all belligerent sides, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Major.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I have no further questions. [Interpretation] Mr. President, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The other Defence team, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I conclude that you don't have any questions for this witness, although your mic was not on when you said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. You are right, we don't have any questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. In light of the questions put to the witness by the Judges and by the Defence, would the Prosecution have one or two questions to put to the witness, Mrs. Benjamin?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution has no questions to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mrs. Benjamin. Major, your testimony is over. You have replied to the questions put to you by the Prosecution, by the Defence, and by the Judges. We thank you for having come to The Hague to testify about these facts. We wish you a safe trip home, and we wish you a lot of success in your current position with the army. We thank you once again. I would like to ask the usher to accompany you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are over with what we had scheduled for today. Would the Prosecution like to raise any issues at this point in time? Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I will simply alert Your Honours and the Defence to the fact that the witness scheduled for tomorrow in fact will be testifying tomorrow, and we do, Mr. President, at this time have copies of Prosecution Exhibit 11, both in the original B/C/S and with the English translation, again consisting of the cover page and the English translations of pages 24 and 25, as previously discussed this morning. And the Prosecution has nothing further for today, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Mundis. At this stage, would the Defence lawyer have anything to say? Mr. Bourgon or Mrs. Residovic? I am giving you the floor for anything you may wish to raise.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, we don't have any issues to raise at this stage, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The other Defence team? Mr. Ibrisimovic, is this anything you would like to say to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We don't have any questions or issues to raise today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We are adjourned for today. Tomorrow we are scheduled to start with the witness Mats Torping, and on Friday we will finish the week with the cross-examination of Mr. Garrod, who started his testimony a little while ago. Thank you very much. And I invite you to come back at 9.00 tomorrow, hoping there won't be any technical problems tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 27th day of May, 2004, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 11.46 a.m.,
